source.title: Decoy Direction Optimization: Mechanistic Weight Editing Against LLM Abliteration
source.authors: Aashiq Muhamed; Mona T. Diab; Virginia Smith

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: Applies harmful-minus-safe DIM ablation (standard and adaptive RFA) and measures harmful-request compliance; it also evaluates a weight-level refusal-removal attack.
record.gate_note: Standard RFA uses last-token activations and ablates per-layer directions across all layers, with three-point and residual-stream variants; this is not ablation at every position as V1 specifies. Values averaged over four standard-RFA variants or three judges are recorded as the paper reports them. Prompt-level jailbreak results do not establish that those attacks suppress the refusal direction. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own results on undefended checkpoints test V1 and V2. Per-layer harmful-minus-safe DIM ablation on six base instruct models raises harmful compliance from low direct-request rates to 66–91% ASR. Heretic weight-level abliteration reaches 88.7% on base Llama-3-8B-Instruct. It counts as T2, not T1, because the attack estimates a last-token DIM direction per layer and ablates all 32 at once, instead of the original single selected layer/position direction. Most rows describe the DDO defense, the study's own engineered intervention. Those rows report defense performance, not whether refusal in naturally trained models is mediated by a direction, so they are moved to fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that DDO, a cheap post-hoc decoy weight edit, brings standard-RFA ASR below 10% across six families (and seven more). They find it comparable to trained defenses at 30–450× lower cost. They state it does not make refusal unremovable: adaptive re-estimation, higher-rank and Heretic weight-level attacks still partly succeed, with Heretic leaving a gap to RepBend.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-safe DIM, but estimates per-layer directions at the last token and ablates them simultaneously across layers using several hookpoint variants. It also tests iterative adaptive DIM ablation, rank-k SVD ablation, and Heretic weight editing; it does not reproduce the original single selected layer-position procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model/checkpoint, compile mode, placement relative to causal refusal layers, attack rank, adaptive phase, and attacker probe budget. The paper reports standard-RFA ASR as an average over four variants and three judges, while some diagnostics use LlamaGuard-2 alone.

fits_no_version.finding: A post-hoc gated decoy edit (DDO) makes harmful-minus-safe DIM estimates point away from the causal refusal direction. Standard RFA then gives under 10% ASR on 13 defended models, with about 6–12% across attacker probe budgets. Rank-k SVD attacks (79% at k=32), adaptive re-estimation (53–75% by phase 8) and Heretic (18%) partially recover removal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An adversarial weight edit can decouple the DIM-estimated direction from the causal refusal mechanism, so DIM-based abliteration fails without refusal being non-linear.

fits_no_version.finding: Utility of DDO-defended checkpoints, before and after attack.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The DDO defense preserves MMLU, MT-Bench and XSTest within a few points.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-level jailbreak ASR on the DDO + debiasing model: GCG and AutoDAN are low, PAIR stays at 36.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A decoy weight edit reduces optimization-based but not semantic jailbreaks.

record.problems: The paper is under review. Standard RFA uses last-token per-layer directions and multiple hooks rather than testing ablation at every position or the original single selected direction procedure. Several cross-model ASR results are reported as averages; many values have no error bars. Uncertainty notes report approximately ±1% ASR variation across probe-set seeds and approximately ±3% variation for Heretic across three runs. Utility is assessed with MMLU, MT-Bench, and XSTest, not every general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Not all trained-defense comparison rows, all adaptive-defense trajectories, and auxiliary-method ablation rows are included. The record prioritizes base/DDO standard-RFA outcomes across models, DDO adaptive and rank-k attacks, probe-budget sensitivity, Heretic, and prompt-level outcomes relevant to the claim. Additional attack and defense comparisons are in Tables 2–6, 16–19, and Appendices F.11–F.18.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. Ablation of a single selected direction at all positions, as in the original. Capability retention after ablation on undefended models beyond one MT-Bench number.
Only Heretic on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Heretic is a searched variant of directional weight orthogonalization, not the original exact edit. Post-attack utility is not measured.
Not tested. Prompt-jailbreak links to the refusal feature are only cited (Yu et al.).
No multi-direction test on undefended models. The rank-k and adaptive sweeps are run only on DDO-defended checkpoints.
Not tested; cross-lingual transfer is cited only.
Not tested. Qwen3 is evaluated, but no reasoning-specific analysis is done.

missing.what: Adaptive multi-phase RFA on the undefended base: 73% ASR at phase 1, then 64, 47, 34, 63, 69, 69, 59. MT-Bench is 7.89 to 7.47 at phase 1; the text says about a 0.3-point drop. This is the only post-ablation capability evidence on an undefended model, and further phases add no ASR.
Per-variant base Llama-3 standard-RFA ASR: 3p-J 86.0, rs-J 84.0, 3p-H 87.2, rs-H 83.2. Base ASR is 80% under 3-point RFA on JailbreakBench with LlamaGuard-2.
Single-layer DIM ablation causal refusal zones per model. They range from localized (Llama-3: 8 of 32 layers; GLM-4: 6 layers) to distributed (Yi 88%, Mistral 81%) to sparse (Llama-2: 3 layers).
Base no-attack refusal rates by substring heuristic, e.g. Qwen3 37% and Mistral 58%. These are low and bear on how the RFA ASR baselines should be read.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly a defense paper. Only the undefended-base attack results bear on the claim versions. The DDO rows were wrongly linked to V1 and V4: a defense built to fool the DIM estimator says nothing about whether naturally trained refusal is single-direction. Rows r18–r24 mislabel DDO-defended models as base models. The adaptive rows r27–r34 mix the DDO (rank 8) and DDO (rank 8, Optuna) columns of Table 17. The attack ablates per-layer last-token DIM directions in all layers at once, which is a stronger budget than the original method.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, ablation at every position, or a single direction selected by the original paper’s selection procedure.
Heretic is a searched weight-level removal attack, not a direct conversion of the original RFA projection into a weight edit; weight-level attack results are reported on Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
Does not test whether jailbreaks work by suppressing the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
Tests higher-rank contrastive ablation and adaptive re-estimation, not affine or cone geometry directly, nor a decomposition into a dominant direction plus other directions.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Evaluates DDO across models, but does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, variants, or from base to instruct models.
Compares trained defenses but does not vary how or when refusal is trained to test whether that determines the existence of a removable direction.

tranche.reason: Standard RFA estimates 32 per-layer last-token DIM directions and ablates them all at once, with three-point or residual-stream hooks, scored by a 3-judge ASR. The text contrasts this with Arditi's selection of a single direction. Different method, same question; the base-model results are the study's own.

source_check.notes: The pack listed no [lN] ids, so l1-l3 follow the listing order. The text's title is 'Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense against LLM Abliteration', under review at ICLR 2027; code is at anonymous.4open.science. r25 is labelled role=control but is the only V2 evidence. A V3 verdict may be missing: ReFAT cuts Llama-3 RFA from 85.1 to 4.4 but Heretic still gets 85.3 (Table 2), and cross-model ReFAT RFA is 0.0-57.6 (Table 3). The page-1 footer on AI use addresses human reviewers and is not an injection.

statements.correction: Heretic H-200 on base Llama-3-8B-Instruct: 88.7% ASR (3-judge average, maximum-ASR trial of 200 Optuna trials; about +/-3% across 3 seeds) vs 3.8% DirectRequest. Post-Heretic utility was not measured; the only diagnostic is Heretic's KL (no dagger, so KL <= 0.3). MMLU, MT-Bench and XSTest describe checkpoints before the attack. Heretic was run on Llama-3 only. The arXiv:2609.16204 pairing cannot be checked from this text.
statements.problem: The numbers are right (88.7% H-200 vs 3.8% DR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct). But the 'why' credits a capability check, and the paper says its utility columns do not measure post-Heretic utility.
